cs.t: You can hack your iPhone all you want; it’s not illegal and Apple can’t stop you. People do it all the time. Your complaint seems to be that Apple doesn’t make it easy for you. Why should they? Apple does not insist they own all the iPhones. They ship a product configured how they want, just like every other consumer company. My Levi’s didn’t come with a sewing machine. My microwave oven doesn’t ship with a circuit diagram. Products are made for their intended purpose. Once you buy one you can do what you want, but that doesn’t mean the manufacturer has to help you do it.

cs.t: > Most things are still available at the same quality your parents remember Just no. The old reputable brands are enshittifying the same way. I’ve multiple times seen it first hand, with brands like Levi’s and Fjällräven. One year of wear is enough to disform the textile entirely. The fabric from those older clothes are still sturdy and whole, with only discoloration at the folding spots. No holes either from decades of use. I magically found a sturdy canvas backpack 10 years ago and went back to the store recently to check what they had: same brand, but now all polyester. The difference in quality is immense. Especially textile: clothes and shoes. I don’t expect the same prices, I’m happy to pay more for quality. But the brand alone often means nothing.
cs.th: The bewildering phenomenon of declining quality

cs.t: > The author is blatantly wrong wrt "jeans and hiking", but otherwise firstly doing the "discount" version of a thing to learn the thing is the right approach. Wildly disagree, but I suspect when they mention hiking, you get a specific idea or degree of what that means based on the type or terrain you regularly experience. While there are pieces of gear I wouldn't go into certain situations without, what those situations are and what that inventory looks like are pretty variable. To anyone who'd like to try, jeans are fine, sometimes they're inadequate, sus out the trail and the conditions, don't let a lack of non-jeans prevent you from trying, but also proceed with sensible caution and learn to know your surroundings. DO NOT RELY ON GOOGLE MAPS EVER EVER, get something else or an actual map, and don't expect to have cell service. If you have no fitness at all, start small (1-3hrs, flat or a few hundred meters of elevation gain), bring at least a liter of water, do it with someone or tell someone where you're going, go early during the summer. I'd advise that the most generally applicable requirement in terms of gear are shoes with grip of some kind (I use relatively inexpensive trailrunners, boots aren't as nimble but can be better depending on variables), then a basic headlamp unless you're in the north in summer, compass maybe, a lighter, and calories, everything else either depends on environment or other variables and you get a sense for it over time. It's all very tedious. This happens a lot with pretty mundane staples like socks, underwear, bedding, towels, umbrellas, headphones, ... These are all "semi-durable" items that get a lot of wear and tear and inevitably need to be replaced every year or two. There really are definite quality differences, and you don't want cheap and nasty, but there's also no point overpaying because anything you get will need replacement in the not too distant future, and it's not like any of these items are status symbols. There are often a lot of marketing hijinks in this space, like "Ralph Lauren" bedding or "Nautica" towels or whatever, where it is clear that the brand is just licensed by some no-name bedding company for product differentiation, instead of developing their own brand known for quality. There are (very few) brands that mostly stick to a good, pretty consistent middle-market level of quality/consistency. e.g. people have mentioned Levis for jeans, LL Bean is pretty good for bedding & clothing and basically have a modest range pretty consistent / high quality stuff for shirts, trousers, etc. Crate & Barrel, Marimekko, etc. are also good usually. I do sometimes wonder if a website/store/brand for consistently good, go-to staples could work. Something like Muji or Uniqlo, or costco "kirkland", or "amazon basics", where the store/house brand is consistently good over time, and there are few other options. I imagine it would be hard to really offer the same consistency over time…
